newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: West set to build nuclear plants in North Korea.
newsitem.headline: West set to build nuclear plants in North Korea.

text.p: A South Korean ship carrying 81 Western diplomats, journalists and South Korean contractors left for North Korea on Monday to mark the "historic" construction of nuclear plants there, Seoul officials said.
They will attend the ground-breaking ceremony, scheduled for 2.00 p.m. (0500 GMT) on Tuesday in the northeastern town of Kumho for two light-water nuclear reactors.
Aboard the vessel Hanara were senior representatives of the United States, South Korea and Japan as well as other members of the Korean Peninsula Energy Development Organisation (KEDO).

KEDO was formed in 1995 by Seoul, Washington and Tokyo after a landmark U.S.-North Korean agreement. It calls for the construction of light-water reactors in return for Pyongyang's promise to halt its suspected atomic weapons programme.
KEDO was later expanded to include Australia, Canada, Chile, Finland, Indonesia, New Zealand and the European Union.
"It is a historic event," said South Korean foreign ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung, referring to the ground-breaking ceremony on Tuesday.
"For the first time since the division of the Korean peninsula, such a large-scale project is being implemented in the isolated North Korea," Lee said.
South Korean officials said they hoped the $4.5 billion project would help reduce tensions on the Korean peninsula and lead to other cooperation between Seoul and Pyongyang.
The two Korea, separated at the end of World War Two, have been locked in Cold War confrontation since the 1950-53 Korean War.

"If the light-water reactor project is successfully implemented, it would contribute to peace and stability on the Korean peninsula," Chang Sun-sup, chief South Korean delegate, told reporters before getting aboard the Hanara.
The KEDO project, which is financed largely by South Korea, has already led to exchanges of mail and telephone linke-up across the heavily fortified Demilitarised Zone bisecting the peninsula.

On Sunday, the first mail from an official of the Korea Electric Power Company (KEPCO) arrived in the South Korean company's headquarter in Seoul. KEPCO is the main contractor for the construction of the reactors.

On August 4, North Korea linked eight telephone lines to the South to allow southern workers preparing to build the nuclear plants to communicate with their families and their headquarters in the South.
Last month, South Korea shipped 9,000 tonnes of bulldozers, trucks and heavy equipment to Kumho to clear land at the project site.
The ground-breaking ceremony coincides with efforts to bring peace to the peninsula and growing fears that chronic food shortages in North Korea will worsen.

Officials of the two Koreas, the United States and China met in New York earlier this month to set an agenda for formal four-nation peace talks but failed to reach an agreement. They are due to try again on September 15 in New York.

The four-nation talks, proposed by Seoul and Washington last year, aim to work out a peace treaty to replace the armistice that only halted fighting, but not the war itself, in the 1950-53 Korean conflict.
